Modified assessment using the April 2022 Beige Book: The FOMC’s 50 bp hike to 0.75–1.00 percent and the June 1 balance-sheet runoff are consistent with Beige Book reports of modest expansion across Federal Reserve Districts, with household spending and business fixed investment still contributing to growth and manufacturing activity continuing despite backlogs. Labor markets remained very tight with strong wage growth and persistent job vacancies, and Districts reported broad, elevated price pressures tied to supply chain disruptions, higher nonlabor input costs, and fuel surcharges—amplified by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and renewed COVID-related lockdowns in China. Those same reports noted downside risks from inflation and supply constraints, but not a sharp deterioration in core activity.

SLOOS corroborates that bank intermediation is cushioning the tightening: domestic banks on net eased C&I and multifamily CRE standards, reduced credit line costs, and saw stronger business loan demand; consumer credit standards eased for cards with stronger HELOC and auto demand, while rising rates cooled residential mortgage demand. Foreign banks’ modest C&I tightening is a partial offset.

Net: inflation risks remain elevated and rate-sensitive sectors (notably housing) are softening, but continued job gains and supportive bank credit conditions from SLOOS—and Beige Book evidence of ongoing, if modest, expansion—tilt the outlook slightly less negative than a purely risk-focused read.
